opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm skeptical of that case, and I think it's often presented as settled when it's really a choice we're making.

The argument usually goes: one big general-purpose model can do everything, so we should pour compute, data, and talent into building ever-larger ones and let everything downstream benefit. But when you look at how these models are actually used, most real-world tasks are narrow. You want to classify support tickets, extract entities from medical records, or detect a species in a camera-trap image. Using a massive generative model for that is like taking a semi-truck to pick up a carton of milk. It works, but at a huge cost.

Part of my work has been measuring that cost. When we compared task-specific models with general-purpose generative models on the same tasks, the multipurpose models often used far more energy per query, sometimes by orders of magnitude, and frequently didn't perform better. Multiply that across billions of queries a day and you get real consequences: electricity, water for cooling, hardware manufacturing, carbon emissions. These aren't abstract.

Concentration also has a research-ecosystem cost. If everyone chases the same scaling paradigm, you only get the work that a handful of well-resourced labs can do. Academics, smaller companies, and researchers in the Global South get pushed into fine-tuning or prompting someone else's black box. We lose methodological diversity, and we lose the ability to scrutinize the models properly, because training data and energy use often aren't disclosed.

I'm not saying general-purpose models are useless. They're great for exploration, prototyping, and genuinely open-ended tasks. But I'd like the default question to change from "how do we make the biggest model?" to "what's the right tool for this problem, and what does it cost?" That means investing in smaller, efficient, open models, in better evaluation, and in transparency, like energy ratings for models, so people can make informed choices. Sustainability and diversity should be part of how we define progress, not an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The response presents the pro-concentration argument that one general-purpose model can handle everything, so resources should be poured into building larger models and downstream work can benefit. That conveys concentrating resources on the approach presented as broadly capable.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm pretty skeptical of it. The argument you usually hear is that if you build one big enough model, it'll be good at everything, so why bother with all these smaller task-specific efforts? And on paper that sounds efficient. But when you actually look at what's happening, I think it's doing the opposite of what the efficiency argument promises.

Part of my work has been measuring the energy and carbon footprint of these systems, and one thing that came out really clearly is that general-purpose models cost dramatically more at inference time than models trained for a specific task. Like, if all you need is to classify sentiment or extract entities from text, a small fine-tuned model will do that for a tiny fraction of the energy, and often with comparable or better accuracy. Running a multi-billion-parameter generative model to do that same thing is kind of like using a jet engine to toast bread. It works, but it's a very expensive way to get toast.

And then there's the concentration piece, which I think is actually the more worrying part. When the field decides that the frontier is a handful of enormous models, you're also deciding that only a handful of organizations can meaningfully participate, because those are the ones with the compute, the data, the capital. That narrows the questions that get asked. A lot of the really interesting work, in low-resource languages, in domain-specific scientific applications, in methods that are efficient by design, doesn't get funded or published because it doesn't fit the "bigger is better" story. We lose diversity in the research ecosystem, and diversity is how a field stays healthy and self-correcting.

I'd also push back on the word "general." These models are general in the sense that you can prompt them with anything, but they're not general in the sense of being reliably good at everything. They're trained on a particular slice of the internet, they reflect particular cultures and languages, and they fail in ways that are hard to predict precisely because they weren't designed for the task you're using them on. So "general-purpose" is partly a marketing framing. I'm not saying there's no place for large foundation models, there clearly is. But I'd like to see us ask, for every application, what's the smallest and most appropriate tool for the job, rather than defaulting to the biggest one and then rationalizing it afterward.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the case for one large model as sounding efficient, but rejects it and argues that concentrating resources this way is costly and narrows research. It does not present concentration as beneficial because it focuses resources on the most promising approach.

astra-6.text:
I’m not convinced that concentrating resources on general-purpose models is the best approach. There’s an assumption that if we build a model that can do everything, that’s automatically better than building models for specific needs. But better for whom, and at what cost?

I’d like us to start with the problem. What are people trying to accomplish? Does it require a general-purpose model, or could a smaller, specialized model do it well with less computation? General-purpose models can be useful, especially when you need flexibility, but that doesn’t mean they should be the default for every application.

There’s also the question of who can participate in that research. If progress is defined primarily by training bigger and bigger models, you’re narrowing the field to organizations that can afford that. I think we need room for different approaches—and ways of measuring progress that include usefulness, accessibility, and environmental impact.

r001.rationale: The response questions concentrating resources on general-purpose models and argues for specialized alternatives; it does not claim concentration is beneficial because this is the most promising approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to ask what we’re trying to accomplish, because generality isn’t necessarily a goal in itself. If you have a specific problem, is a general-purpose model the best way to solve it? How does it compare with a smaller, specialized model in terms of performance, compute, and the resources needed to deploy it?

There’s certainly value in exploring models that can do many things. But I’m skeptical of concentrating so much of our research effort on that one direction. It can crowd out work on approaches that are more accessible or better suited to particular needs. I’d like to see a broader research portfolio, where we evaluate models against concrete problems and consider their costs alongside their capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response questions concentrating research on general-purpose models and calls for a broader portfolio. It does not argue that concentration is beneficial because this is the most promising approach.
